Last but not least, we have applied a soft bootstrap approach to these condensed matter systems. In this analysis we take as input the assumption of an enhanced Adler zero condition for soft NGBs. While we have identified exceptional theories of the solid and fluid with these enhanced infrared properties, they are all closely related in structure to relativistic DBI.

Our analysis leaves a number of directions for future work. For example, as noted earlier, our soft theorem does not actually require $SO(3)$ rotation invariance in the broken phase. Indeed, the only requirement is that symmetry breaking preserves some notion of a conserved energy and momentum. For this reason one can in principle study condensed matter systems with even less rotational symmetry. It would be interesting to classify these theories and their corresponding soft theorems.

Throughout this paper we have focused on scattering induced by the self-interactions of phonons. However, the interactions of phonons with other degrees of freedom, e.g., crystal defects or vortices are also of interest for many condensed matter systems. As long as these other modes can be incorporated consistently into the EFT of spontaneous spacetime symmetry breaking, it should be possible to mechanically derive new soft theorems for scattering processes involving these other degrees of freedom.

Another avenue for exploration is more elaborate variations of the soft bootstrap. In particular, it should be possible to assume a general ansatz for the broken symmetry parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$ , as well as a general ansatz for the propagator and cubic vertex, $\Delta$ and $V_{3}$ . Sculpting out the space of amplitudes satisfying our soft theorem might offer insight into new condensed matter systems of interest.

Finally, it would be interesting to understand whether the geometric perspective on soft theorems presented in [59, 60] extends to a nonrelativistic setting. A geometric description of the corresponding EFTs has already been described in [26], so generalizing to this case should be relatively straightforward.

## Appendix A Nonrelativistic Kinematics

Our analysis will require a careful treatment of on-shell kinematics for scattering amplitudes with nonrelativistic dynamics. For the $n$ -point amplitude, $A_{n}$ , we define the four-momenta of the $n$ hard legs to be

$$ \displaystyle p_{a}^{\mu}=(\omega_{a},{p}_{a}^{i})\,, $$

where the external particle index is an integer in the range $1\leq a\leq n$ .

It will be crucial to define the notion of a minimal on-shell basis of kinematic invariants. A priori, the $n$ -point amplitude is an $SO(3)$ invariant quantity that is a function of the energies $\omega_{a}$ and all inner products of three-momenta, ${p}_{a}\cdot{p}_{b}$ for $1\leq a\leq b\leq n$ . A minimal on-shell basis defines a set of kinematic variables for which all on-shell constraints are automatically imposed.

To achieve this, we first eliminate the energy and three-momentum of some leg, chosen here to be leg $n$ , so

$$ \displaystyle\omega_{n}=-\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}\omega_{a}\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad{p}_{n}^{i}=-\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}p_{a}^{i}\,. $$

The elimination of the energy $\omega_{n}$ and three-momentum ${p}_{n}^{i}$ of leg $n$ via the above equations then automatically enforces total momentum conservation. Second, we impose the on-shell conditions for the external legs, allowing us to eliminate the kinematic invariants

$$ \displaystyle{p}_{a}^{2}=\frac{\omega_{a}^{2}}{c_{a}^{2}}\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 1\leq a\leq n-1\,, $$

where $c_{a}$ is the speed of sound for the corresponding leg. For example, for phonons it would be the longitudinal or transverse speeds of sound, $c_{L}$ or $c_{T}$ . The above condition allows us to eliminate ${p}_{a}^{2}$ for $1\leq a\leq n-1$ . However since we have already eliminated ${p}_{n}^{i}$ by momentum conservation, for the case of $a=n$ the on-shell condition imposes a more elaborate constraint,

$$ \displaystyle{p}_{n}^{2}=\left(\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}{p}_{a}\right)^{2}=\frac{1}{c_{n}^{2}}\left(\sum_{a=1}^{n-1}\omega_{a}\right)^{2}\,, $$

which should can be used to eliminate one more kinematic invariant, which we can choose to be ${p}_{n-2}\cdot{p}_{n-1}$ without loss of generality. In summary, the minimal kinematic basis is comprised of the variables

$$ \displaystyle\omega_{a} \displaystyle\textrm{for}\qquad 1\leq a\leq n-1\,, \displaystyle{p}_{a}\cdot{p}_{b} \displaystyle\textrm{for}\qquad 1\leq a<b\leq n-2\qquad\textrm{and}\qquad 1\leq a\leq n-3,\;\;b=n-1\,, $$

with all other kinematic variables fixed by on-shell conditions.

With the inclusion of external polarization vectors, ${e}_{a}^{i}$ for $1\leq a\leq n$ , similar logic applies. Without assuming any special properties of the external polarizations, for example whether they are longitudinal or transverse, we simply eliminate all invariants involving ${p}_{n}^{i}$ . Hence, we obtain

$$ \displaystyle{e}_{a}\cdot{e}_{b} \displaystyle\textrm{for}\qquad 1\leq a<b\leq n\,, \displaystyle{p}_{a}\cdot{e}_{b} \displaystyle\textrm{for}\qquad 1\leq a\leq n-1,\;\;1\leq b\leq n\,, $$

for the elements of the minimal kinematic basis involving polarizations.

Let us also write down the explicit minimal kinematic basis for three-point scattering,

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{ basis for }A_{3}: \displaystyle\omega_{1},\,\;\omega_{2}\,, \displaystyle{\displaystyle p}_{1}\cdot{e}_{1},\,\;{p}_{1}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{p}_{1}\cdot{e}_{3},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e}_{1},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e}_{3}\,, \displaystyle{\displaystyle e}_{1}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{e}_{1}\cdot{e}_{3},\,\;{e}_{2}\cdot{e}_{3}\,. $$

The utility of these variables is that we can freely change them while remaining on the kinematic surface that defines on-shell configurations. From here on, we will write all on-shell quantities in terms of these minimal bases.

Finally, to evaluate the amplitude for a specific configuration of external modes, we plug in explicit longitudinal or transverse polarizations. The trasverse conditions put additional constraints on the minimal basis

$$ \displaystyle{p}_{a}\cdot{e}_{a} \displaystyle=0\qquad\textrm{for}\qquad 1\leq a<n\,, \displaystyle{p}_{n-1}\cdot{e}_{n} \displaystyle=-\sum_{a=1}^{n-2}{p}_{a}\cdot{e}_{n}\,. $$

For our analysis, we will be interested in how the soft limit of the $(n+1)$ -point amplitude, $A_{n+1}$ , can be expressed in terms of the $n$ -point amplitude, $A_{n}$ . For this reason, we define legs $1,\cdots,n$ to be hard, since they are present in both $A_{n+1}$ and $A_{n}$ . On the other hand, leg $n+1$ , with external polarization $e^{i}$ , will be taken soft, so we parameterize it with a special four-momentum

$$ \displaystyle q^{\mu}=(\omega,{q}^{i})\,. $$

To be very explicit, $A_{n+1}$ is a function of $p_{1},\cdots,p_{n},q$ while $A_{n}$ is a function of ${,}\cdots,p_{n}$ . Both should be evaluated in a minimal kinematic basis in which the energy $\omega_{n}$ , the three-momentum ${p}_{n}^{i}$ , and the invariant ${p}_{n-2}\cdot{p}_{n-1}$ have been eliminated. Consequently, for any values of the soft momentum $q$ , the amplitudes remain on-shell. This ensures that the soft limit is taken while maintaining all on-shell conditions. The minimal basis for four-point scattering is then

$$ \displaystyle\textrm{ basis for }A_{4}: \displaystyle\omega,\,\;\omega_{1},\,\;\omega_{2},\,\;{q}\cdot{p}_{1},\,\;{q}\cdot{p}_{2},\,\;{q}\cdot{e},\,\;{q}\cdot{e}_{1},\,\;{q}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{q}\cdot{e}_{3}\,, \displaystyle{\displaystyle p}_{1}\cdot{e},\,\;{p}_{1}\cdot{e}_{1},\,\;{p}_{1}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{p}_{1}\cdot{e}_{3},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e}_{1},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{p}_{2}\cdot{e}_{3}\,, \displaystyle{\displaystyle e}\cdot{e}_{1},\,\;{e}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{e}\cdot{e}_{3},\,\;{e}_{1}\cdot{e}_{2},\,\;{e}_{1}\cdot{e}_{3},\,\;{e}_{2}\cdot{e}_{3}\,. $$

By construction, the minimal basis for $A_{4}$ in Eq. (A.10) reduces to the minimal basis for $A_{3}$ in Eq. (A.7) in the soft limit, $q\rightarrow 0$ .

While the above approach is somewhat convoluted, we emphasize that any definition of the soft limit of an on-shell amplitude requires something analogous. In general, simply changing the momentum $q$ of a leg to be soft will not maintain on-shell conditions. For the case of on-shell soft recursion [39, 61, 41, 62], the soft limit of a given leg must always be compensated by a slight shift of one of the hard legs. The minimal basis construction we have described above achieves this automatically.

# Soft phonon theorems

Cliﬀord Cheung, Maria Derda, Andreas Helset and Julio Parra-Martinez

Walter Burke Institute for Theoretical Physics, California Institute of Technology, 1200 E California Blvd, Pasadena, CA 91125, U.S.A.

E-mail: clifford.cheung@caltech.edu, mderda@caltech.edu, ahelset@gmail.com, jparram@caltech.edu

Abstract: A variety of condensed matter systems describe gapless modes that can be interpreted as Nambu-Goldstone bosons of spontaneously broken Poincaré symmetry. In this paper we derive new soft theorems constraining the tree-level scattering of these degrees of freedom, as exhibited in solids, ﬂuids, superﬂuids, and framids. These soft theorems are in one-to-one correspondence with various broken symmetries, including spacetime translations, Lorentz boosts, and, for the case of ﬂuids, volume-preserving diﬀeomorphisms. We also implement a bootstrap in which the enhanced vanishing of amplitudes in the soft limit is taken as an input, thus sculpting out a subclass of exceptional solid, ﬂuid, and framid theories.

Keywords: Eﬀective Field Theories, Scattering Amplitudes, Space-Time Symmetries

## 1 Introduction

The seminal work of Nambu and Goldstone [1–3] revealed a deep connection between spontaneously broken internal symmetries and a corresponding set of gapless degrees of freedom. These Nambu-Goldstone bosons (NGBs) parameterize a continuous degeneracy of vacua and transform nonlinearly under the broken symmetries. Notably, spontaneous symmetry breaking often mandates universal features in scattering, as perhaps best illustrated by the Adler zero [4], which refers to the vanishing of certain NGB amplitudes in the soft limit. As is well-known, similar statements apply to the spontaneous breaking of spacetime symmetries [5–9], albeit with a fewer number of NGBs than naively expected [10–13]. More recently, it has also been suggested that spontaneous breaking of Poincaré invariance is not merely a calling card of certain condensed matter systems, but can actually be elevated to an organizing principle for these theories [14]. In this approach, nonrelativistic eﬀective ﬁeld theories (EFTs) are classiﬁed by their spacetime symmetry breaking pattern, yielding a rich array of physical systems corresponding to the phonon excitations at zero temperature of perfect solids and ﬂuids, as well as modes of a superﬂuid. The authors of [14] also discovered some exotic, yet-to-be-experimentally-realized systems which include the framid, whose corresponding framon degree of freedom exhibits the minimal nonlinear realization of spontaneous Lorentz symmetry breaking. In this paper we study the soft behavior of scattering amplitudes of NGBs arising from the spontaneous breaking of spacetime symmetries. Our analysis focuses on the nonrelativistic EFTs classiﬁed in [14] by the symmetry breaking pattern corresponding to solids, ﬂuids, superﬂuids, and framids. In all of these systems, the group of spatial rotations is preserved at low energies, so the NGBs reside in a linear representation of SO(3). For example, the superﬂuid phonon is described by a scalar ﬁeld π, while solid and ﬂuid phonons and framons are described by a three-vector ﬁeld πi.1 In general, the latter NGBs nonlinearly realize the underlying broken spacetime symmetries via

πi →πi + αi + βi jπj + · · · , (1.1)

for parameters α and β, which are in general position-dependent, and where the ellipses denote terms higher order in the ﬁeld. In our analysis, we focus primarily on the case in which the broken spacetime symmetry generators are translations or boosts, but also consider the case of broken spatial diﬀeomorphisms in a ﬂuid.

For products of three-momenta we will sometimes employ the shorthand, p · q = piqi.

Technically, our results apply to any symmetry breaking pattern involving spacetime or internal symmetries or both.2 The schematic form of our soft theorem is

(1.2) are O(q0) in the soft momentum, which is to say that terms O(q1) or higher have been dropped. The summations above run over all external legs in An, which are assumed to be hard. Since α and β are in general functions of spacetime, they act as diﬀerential operators on the external momenta. In particular, in eq. (1.2), α acts on the soft energy or momentum, while β acts on the energy or momenta of each hard leg in An. Depending on the diﬀerential degree of α and β, they will extract diﬀerent powers in the soft expansion of the amplitudes. For example, if α is a constant, then eq. (1.2) extracts the O(q0) piece of An+1, while if α is a single derivative with respect to the soft energy or momentum, then it probes the O(q1) piece of An+1. Eq. Furthermore, as required of any physical on-shell scattering, the soft theorem in eq. (1.2) is satisﬁed irrespective of the choice of ﬁeld basis. This feature is actually rather miraculous when one considers that eq. (1.2) depends explicitly on the oﬀ-shell three-point vertex V3, which is ﬁeld basis dependent along with the symmetry parameter β. However, as we will later argue, any change of ﬁeld basis that sends V3 and β to an alternative choice of V ′ 3 and β′ necessarily cancels in the soft theorem. The fact that the soft theorem is on-shell makes our results distinct from the soft theorems for correlation functions derived in [16–20]. The structure of this paper is as follows. In section 2 we state the general soft theorem and present a proof as well as a discussion of its invariance under changes of ﬁeld basis. We then turn to concrete examples of theories that satisfy the soft theorem: superﬂuids in section 3, solids in section 4, ﬂuids in section 5, and framids in section 6. In section 7 we discuss a soft bootstrap for nonrelativistic theories, and we conclude in section 8.

### 2.3 Field basis independence

Next, we show how the soft theorem in eq. (2.25) is invariant under changes of ﬁeld basis. To begin, we clarify that there are actually two physically distinct senses in which a soft theorem can be considered ﬁeld basis invariant. The ﬁrst sense is simply the statement that the soft theorem is valid irrespective of which ﬁeld basis the quantities β and V3 are deﬁned in, which enter explicitly into eq. (2.25). If we transform to a diﬀerent ﬁeld basis, these quantities will change to β′ and V ′ 3. But crucially, all of the manipulations in the previous section still hold. Hence the soft theorem will still apply, so its validity is ﬁeld basis independent. The second sense is more nontrivial, and it is the statement that the on-shell amplitudes An+1 and An can be computed in diﬀerent ﬁeld bases and the soft theorems will still be satisﬁed. As is well-known, changes of ﬁeld basis induce new terms which always vanish on-shell in the amplitudes. However, since our soft theorems involve diﬀerential operators in energy and momentum, one can worry whether these vanishing terms end up contributing

## 7 Soft bootstrap

Our analysis thus far has focused on incarnations of the soft theorem in eq. (2.25), which relate nonzero expressions involving the (n + 1)-point and n-point amplitudes. However, in the special circumstance where soft limits vanish — also known as Adler zeros — the corresponding theories typically exhibit enhanced symmetry structures. Concretely, the Adler zero stipulates that

lim q→0 An+1(p1, · · · , pn, q) = O(q1) , (7.1)

<!-- Page 23 -->


JHEP08(2023)103

which is the case for, e.g., amplitudes of pions in the NLSM [4]. In special circumstances, scalar EFTs can exhibit an enhanced Adler zero,

lim q→0 An+1(p1, · · · , pn, q) = O(q2) . (7.2)

This is the case for Dirac-Born-Infeld (DBI) theory and the Galileon. Remarkably, the NLSM, DBI, and the Galileon exhibit a soft behavior of amplitudes that is enhanced beyond what is naively expected simply from counting the number of derivatives per interaction vertex. Hence, by writing an ansatz and imposing eq. (7.1) or eq. (7.2) as constraints, one can bootstrap these theories from ﬁrst principles [36–39]. These resulting theories have highly constrained interactions, and were dubbed exceptional scalar EFTs. The soft bootstrap has also been extended to broader classes of theories, including theories with vectors or fermions [40–54] as well as nonrelativistic theories [55–57]. In the context of spacetime symmetry breaking, it is natural to ask: Are there exceptional nonrelativistic EFTs? Are there exceptional theories of phonons and framons?

### 7.1 Exceptional phonons

We start by considering eﬀective theories of phonons, i.e., corresponding to spacetime symmetry breaking pattern of solids, ﬂuids, and superﬂuids, which all have interaction vertices with one derivative per ﬁeld. First, we want to establish the Adler zero for these theories, i.e., the requirement that the amplitudes vanish as O(q1) in the soft limit. For a theory with one derivative per ﬁeld, all interaction vertices involving the soft particle will scale as O(q1). This suggests that the on-shell amplitudes should also scale as O(q1), thus exhibiting an Adler zero. However, as is well-known, this reasoning fails in the presence of three-point interaction vertices, which generically induce O(q−1) soft poles. These contributions can, in principle, conspire with O(q1) contributions from the interaction vertex to give an amplitude that scales as O(q0). In relativistic theories of derivatively coupled scalars, there are no such soft poles because there are no on-shell three-point amplitudes. The only nonzero three-point amplitude for relativistic scalars is a constant arising from a cubic potential term, which is absent by deﬁnition for derivatively coupled scalars. The absence of relativistic three-point scalar amplitudes implies the existence of a ﬁeld basis where the corresponding three-point vertex is zero and thus there are no singular terms in the soft limit. In contrast, nonrelativistic theories can have nontrivial three-point amplitudes, even in theories with interaction vertices with one derivative per ﬁeld. Thus, the Adler zero is not automatic. A suﬃcient condition for having an Adler zero for such nonrelativistic theories is to demand that all three-point amplitudes vanish.

## 8 Conclusions

In this paper we have initiated a systematic analysis of the soft behavior of scattering amplitudes in a broad class of condensed matter systems. The common thread linking these theories is that their gapless modes are the NGBs of spontaneously broken spacetime symmetries. As per the classiﬁcation of [14], the dynamics of superﬂuids, solids, ﬂuids, and framids can all be derived from universal principles governing nonlinearly realized symmetries. Using current conservation, we have derived the general soft theorem in eq. (2.25), which encodes the action of broken symmetry generators on the NGBs. The ingredients entering the soft theorem are the parameters of the broken symmetry transformation, α and β, together with the propagator and cubic vertex of the theory, ∆and V3. While β and V3 are generally dependent on the ﬁeld basis, and thus not individually invariant, they enter into eq. (2.25) in a way that is ﬁeld basis independent. Furthermore, eq. (2.25) should be viewed as a soft theorem because it is an operation relating on-shell scattering amplitudes. Applying this construction to various EFTs, we present and check a broad array of soft theorems, including those corresponding to temporal translations and Lorentz boosts of the superﬂuid, spatial translations and Lorentz boosts of the solid, volume-preserving diﬀeomorphisms of the ﬂuid, and Lorentz boosts of the framid. Last but not least, we have applied a soft bootstrap approach to these condensed matter systems. In this analysis we take as input the assumption of an enhanced Adler zero condition for soft NGBs. While we have identiﬁed exceptional theories of the solid and ﬂuid with these enhanced infrared properties, they are all closely related in structure to relativistic DBI. Our analysis leaves a number of directions for future work. For example, as noted earlier, our soft theorem does not actually require SO(3) rotation invariance in the broken phase. Indeed, the only requirement is that symmetry breaking preserves some notion of a conserved energy and momentum. For this reason one can in principle study condensed matter systems with even less rotational symmetry. It would be interesting to classify these theories and their corresponding soft theorems. Throughout this paper we have focused on scattering induced by the self-interactions of phonons. However, the interactions of phonons with other degrees of freedom, e.g., crystal defects or vortices are also of interest for many condensed matter systems. As long as these other modes can be incorporated consistently into the EFT of spontaneous spacetime symmetry breaking, it should be possible to mechanically derive new soft theorems for scattering processes involving these other degrees of freedom. Another avenue for exploration is more elaborate variations of the soft bootstrap. In particular, it should be possible to assume a general ansatz for the broken symmetry

Sculpting out the space of amplitudes satisfying our soft theorem might oﬀer insight into new condensed matter systems of interest. Finally, it would be interesting to understand whether the geometric perspective on soft theorems presented in [61, 62] extends to a nonrelativistic setting. A geometric description of the corresponding EFTs has already been described in [26], so generalizing to this case should be relatively straightforward.

## Abstract

Droplet-based and split-pool barcoding are the two dominant high-throughput single-cell RNA-seq paradigms, yet their systematic biases remain incompletely characterized. We compared seven matched 10X Genomics Chromium and Parse Biosciences Evercode WT sample pairs from five studies spanning multiple tissues and species focusing on gene counts and compositional differences rather than cell-type resolution. By separating Parse reads by priming strategy, we distinguished biases arising from priming chemistry from platform-level effects. These effects were largely independent, with platformlevel differences substantially larger. Priming strategy introduced a GC-content bias within Parse, whereas the two platforms showed a consistent compositional shift across priming strategies, supported by differential capture of nuclear- and cytoplasmic-enriched transcripts. We interpret this shift as a relative enrichment of nuclear RNA in Parse. Finally, using contamination measures that do not assume a droplet-specific model, we found background RNA contamination in Parse to be comparable in magnitude to that in 10X, contrary to claims of substantially lower contamination. Together, these results indicate that expression measurements and cell-type composition are not directly interchangeable between the two platforms.

Keywords: single-cell RNA-seq, split-pool barcoding, technology benchmarking, nuclear RNA capture, priming strategy, GC-content bias, ambient RNA contamination

## Introduction

Over the past couple of decades, single-cell methods have become essential components of biological discovery, as they are uniquely positioned to capture genome-wide molecular variation at the resolution of individual cells (Tanay and Regev, 2017; Kolodziejczyk et al., 2015). Among the several single-cell RNA-seq experimental paradigms, droplet-based and split-pool barcoding technologies are the highest-throughput techniques, able to profile up to millions of cells at a time (Zheng et al., 2017; Rosenberg et al., 2018). Both technologies use physical or conceptual isolation of cells to label each mRNA molecule with a cell barcode and unique molecular identifier (UMI) through a combination of reverse transcription, ligation, and amplification. The resulting cDNA library can then be sequenced and each read assigned to a single cell and molecule during downstream processing.

Droplet-based technologies, commercialized by 10X Genomics, are the older of the two and currently the most widely used (Zheng et al., 2017). With this set of methods, cells and RNA-barcoded beads are separately loaded onto a microfluidics device, which encapsulates a cell and bead pair within a droplet containing lysis buffer. Once encapsulated, the cell lyses in the buffer, releasing RNA that binds to the bead primers and initiates reverse transcription.

In contrast, split-pool barcoding technologies do not physically separate cells (Rosenberg et al., 2018; Cao et al., 2017). Instead, the cells themselves act as the reaction chamber for RNA priming and reverse transcription, and cells are permeabilized to allow reagents into the cytoplasm. Transcripts are uniquely labelled through multiple barcoding rounds. In each round, pooled cells are divided onto a multi-well plate. In the first round, RNA sequences are captured by a DNA primer containing a well-unique barcode and a UMI, then reverse transcribed. In subsequent rounds, a well-unique barcode is ligated onto the end of a cDNA molecule’s existing primer which is then amplified. In an optional final round, cells are divided into sub-libraries before cell lysis, and the Illumina sample indices added during PCR amplification act as an additional barcode. This approach relies on the stochastic combinatorics of the split-pool process to ensure that each cell is labeled with a unique barcode combination with high probability.

Both technologies are now widely in use, particularly in their commercialized forms, and have been shown to perform similarly with respect to distinguishing cell types. However, they also exhibit systematic biases that complicate direct comparison and generalization across platforms. Several points of technical difference between the Parse Biosciences and 10X Genomics kits could plausibly contribute to such biases. The Chromium 3’ kit profiles the contents of live, lysed cells, whereas the Evercode WT kit profiles the contents of formaldehyde-fixed and permeabilized cells. The two encapsulation paradigms also differ in their susceptibility to doublets, barcode collisions, and ambient RNA contamination, all of which are known to distort single-cell data. Finally, the platforms differ in RNA priming strategy: the 10X Chromium kit relies exclusively on oligo(dT) priming of the poly(A) tail common to most mRNA, whereas the Parse Evercode WT kit combines oligo(dT) priming with random hexamer priming, which additionally captures non-polyadenylated RNA species such as certain long non-coding RNAs.

Several studies from different groups, spanning multiple species and tissues, have characterized aspects of these biases, particularly between the 10X Genomics Single-Cell 3’ Chromium kit and the Parse Biosciences Evercode WT kit (Gezelius et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; De Simone et al., 2025; Filippov et al., 2024; Hornung et al., 2023; King et al., 2026; Brown et al., 2024; Sarieva et al., 2026). These studies are difficult to reconcile with one another, as each examines a different subset of features, and none draws on a sufficient number of biological and technical replicates across tissues and species to support a general conclusion. No study to date has attempted to unify these findings into a single, direct comparison.

In this paper, we compare seven matched 10X Genomics Chromium and Parse Biosciences Evercode WT sample pairs spanning multiple tissues, species, and kit versions. Within Parse, we separate oligo(dT)-primed reads from random-hexamer-primed reads to determine the extent to which systematic biases originate from priming strategy rather than from other platform differences. In addition to library-level quality metrics, we perform bulk differential expression and gene ontology analysis to characterize compositional differences in gene capture both between platforms and between priming strategies within Parse. We find that 10X and Parse diverge primarily along an axis consistent with differential nuclear RNA capture, a bias that is largely independent of priming strategy and reproducible across species; we additionally find a smaller, distinct bias between priming strategies within Parse that is best explained by transcript GC content.

## Results

To characterize systematic differences between droplet-based and split-pool single-cell RNA-seq platforms, we compared seven matched 10X Genomics Chromium and Parse Biosciences Evercode WT sample pairs drawn from five previously published studies (Table 1). The datasets span three tissue types (cell lines, peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs), and thymocytes) and three species contexts (human, mouse, and human-mouse mixture). For each experiment, Parse reads were further partitioned by priming strategy into three constituent datasets: reads captured by oligo(dT) priming alone (“Parse 3”’), reads captured by random hexamer priming alone (“Parse randO”), and all Parse reads together (“Parse combined”). Each of the four datasets in a given experiment – 10X, Parse 3’, Parse randO, and Parse combined – was independently subsampled from its own respective pool of reads to the depth of the smallest dataset in that experiment (Figure S1.). This allows for direct comparison of library quality and composition at matched sequencing depth without conflating depth differences with platform or priming differences.

### 10X sequencing results in higher library quality regardless of priming strategy though differences in gene diversity are less clear.

10X libraries were of higher quality than Parse libraries by several measures, regardless of priming strategy. When aligned to either the transcriptome with kallisto (Bray et al., 2016) (Fig. 1A and 1B) or the genome with STAR (Dobin et al., 2013) (Fig. S2A), the 10X library had a lower percentage of unmapped reads and a higher percentage of valid barcodes than the matching Parse libraries. In addition, when reads were aligned to the genome with STAR, 10X libraries yielded a greater number of uniquely mapped reads than any of the three Parse datasets (Fig. S2B). Within Parse, the randO dataset consistently produced the fewest uniquely mapped reads of the three subsampled datasets.

Dot plots showing the range of each kallisto pseudoalignment metric across the subsampled datasets from each experiment: (A) percent of reads unmapped by kallisto; (B) percent of valid barcode combinations recovered by kallisto. Two diversity metrics computed on unfiltered gene counts: (C) shannon entropy over total counts per gene; (D) total genes detected. Experiment labels in (A) and (C) are colored by tissue.*

Several of the studies from which these datasets were drawn report that Parse captures a greater diversity of transcripts than 10X (Filippov et al., 2024; Xie et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2024; Gezelius et al., 2024). Sarieva et al. (2026) is the only study to report a greater number of genes captured by 10X, though we did not analyze their data ourselves. Our results generally support this claim for the majority of experiments analyzed. For almost all experiments, both Shannon entropy (Fig. 1C) and total genes detected (Fig. 1D) were lower for 10X than for Parse combined, with the exception of Experiment 4a and 4b. In Experiment 4a and 4b, 10X showed substantially higher Shannon entropy than all Parse datasets despite detecting fewer total genes, except in Experiment 4b, where 10X detected more genes than Parse 3’. In addition, in Experiment 3, 10X detected more genes than Parse randO.

Across all experiments, the Parse combined dataset detected more genes than either the Parse 3’ or Parse randO datasets alone, consistent with the two priming strategies capturing partially non-overlapping sets of transcripts. We note, however, that because Parse combined is independently subsampled from the full pool of Parse reads rather than constructed as the union of the 3’ and randO datasets, this result is also consistent in part with the combined pool simply being more diverse prior to subsampling.

### Variance between 10X and Parse datasets is dominated by batch effect between platforms.

Across all experiments, 10X and Parse datasets showed high concordance (Fig. 2A), as expected for matched samples profiling the same underlying biology: the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) exceeded 0.8 between 10X and each of the three Parse datasets. However, the variance attributable to platform substantially exceeded the variance attributable to priming strategy within Parse. Across all comparisons, CCC values between any two of the three Parse datasets (3’, randO, and combined) were consistently higher than CCC values between 10X and any individual Parse dataset.

*Fig 2.: Platform contributes more variance between datasets than priming strategy. (A) PCA of unfiltered and shifted-CLR normalized bulk counts for each subsampled dataset from the four human experiments. (B) Heatmaps of the concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) between filtered and logCPM normalized bulk counts for the four datasets within each experiment. Experiment labels are colored by tissue as in Fig. 1.*

This pattern was also evident in a principal component analysis of the filtered, shifted-CLR normalized (Booeshaghi et al., 2026) bulk gene counts across all human datasets (Fig. 2B). PC1 (48.9% of variance) separated PBMC samples from cancer cell line samples, reflecting expected biological differences between sample types. PC2 (23.8% of variance) separated samples by platform, with 10X datasets taking positive values and all three Parse datasets taking negative values. Within a given experiment, Parse 3’ clustered more closely with the Parse randO and Parse combined datasets on PC2 than with 10X, indicating that the platform-driven batch effect dominates over both priming strategy and experiment-of-origin effects within Parse. Parse 3’ datasets were, however, consistently shifted toward more positive PC2 values relative to Parse randO and Parse combined.

Consistent with 10X and Parse 3’ sharing a common priming strategy, CCC values between 10X and Parse 3’ were consistently higher than CCC values between 10X and Parse randO across experiments. These results suggest that the primary source of variation between 10X and Parse is due to platform-level batch effect rather than priming strategies, while differences in priming strategy contribute to batch effect both within and between platforms but to a lesser extent.

### Compositional differences between 10X and Parse are consistent with differential nuclear RNA capture.

Beyond the platform-level batch effect described above, 10X and Parse datasets differed in the relative abundance of several transcript classes (Fig. 3), with Parse exhibiting a bias towards nuclear transcripts. The nucleus is known to contain a greater number of unprocessed transcripts, and within each experiment, the mean percentage of nascent (unspliced) counts per cell was higher in Parse than in 10X. Across experiments, the mean nascent percentage in Parse ranged from 35.88% to 59.85%, compared to 13.81% to 40.70% in 10X, with the Parse 3’ and randO datasets closely tracking the combined Parse range.

Outliers beyond the 5th and 95th percentiles are not shown here. Experiment labels are colored by tissue as in Fig. 1.*

This pattern extended to individual transcripts and to broader RNA classes, and in two cases the platforms separate almost entirely. MALAT1, a transcript retained almost exclusively in the nucleus (Clarke and Bader, 2024), was substantially depleted in 10X relative to Parse: the mean per-cell MALAT1 percentage across 10X datasets ranged from <0.01% to 0.33%, compared to a mean of 1.44% to 4.87% in Parse, with Parse 3’ and randO again tracking the combined Parse range. Conversely, ribosomal protein-coding RNA was depleted in Parse relative to 10X: mean per-cell ribosomal percentage in Parse ranged from 0.44% to 2.15%, compared to a mean of 9.00% to 25.96% in 10X, a trend which was also noted in King et al. (2026) and Sarieva et al. (2026). A similar pattern of depletion held at the level of broader RNA classes: mean per-cell protein-coding percentage ranged from 92.79% to 95.26% in 10X compared to 63.05% to 85.60% in Parse, while mean per-cell long non-coding RNA (lncRNA) percentage ranged from 8.09% to 12.16% in Parse compared to only 3.81% to 4.75% in 10X, a relationship which was also found in Sarieva et al. (2026).

These results are consistent with a shift toward nuclear RNA capture in Parse relative to 10X. The intronic fraction and MALAT1 percentage are both known to be associated with higher nuclear capture (Clarke and Bader, 2024; Muskovic and Powell, 2021). The shift we observe in Parse toward higher MALAT1 percentage, higher intronic read percentage, lower protein-coding percentage, and higher lncRNA percentage parallels differences previously reported between single-nucleus and single-cell RNA-seq, where single-nucleus protocols show the same directional shifts relative to single-cell protocols (Selewa et al., 2020).

In contrast to this nuclear-capture bias, 10X and Parse showed no consistent difference in indicators of cellular damage. Mean per-cell mitochondrial count percentage ranged from 2% to 8% across both platforms and all experiments, with no clear trend distinguishing 10X from Parse; an increase in mitochondrial RNA percentage is generally taken as an indicator of lower cell quality, as the mitochondrial membrane is more resistant to disruption than the plasma membrane and so mitochondrial contents are less likely to be released prior to lysis (Ilicic et al., 2016). The absence of a platform-level difference in mitochondrial percentage suggests that the nuclear-capture bias observed between 10X and Parse reflects a difference in nuclear RNA retention specifically, rather than a general difference in cell quality or damage between the two protocols.

### Differential expression analysis reveals broad shifts in compositional gene expression between technologies.

To further characterize the platform-level bias described above, we performed differential expression analysis with edgePython on the bulk counts from the three human PBMC datasets, blocking on study of origin. Because 10X and Parse 3’ share a common priming strategy, we restricted this comparison to 10X versus Parse 3’ to isolate platform-level effects from priming-level effects.

Despite sharing a priming strategy, 10X and Parse 3’ were readily separable in an MDS plot of the bulk counts (Fig. S3A). Dimension 1 (74.8% of variance) separated 10X from Parse 3’, indicating that platform is the dominant axis of variation even when priming strategy is held constant.

Bulk differential expression analysis identified substantial compositional shifts between platforms: at an FDR threshold of 0.01, 6,346 genes were significantly enriched in 10X and 5,418 in Parse 3’ (Fig. 4A). As a cross-species validation, we asked whether the genes found to be platform-enriched in the human PBMC comparison showed consistent enrichment in an independent pair of mouse thymocyte experiments (Experiments 4a (Fig. 4D) and 4b (Fig. S4A)), which were not part of the original PBMC analysis. For genes significantly enriched in 10X in the PBMC comparison (FDR < 0.01), the mouse orthologs showed higher bulk logCPM in 10X than in Parse 3’: 88.46% in Experiment 4a, and 86.57 in Experiment 4b. The converse held only weakly: for genes enriched in Parse in the PBMC comparison, the orthologs favored Parse in just 61.56% of cases in Experiment 4a and 70.97% in Experiment 4b.

Because RNA-seq methods are known to exhibit GC-content and length biases through several mechanisms, we asked whether either contributed to the differential expression observed between 10X and Parse 3’. Both GC content (Fig. 4B) and median transcript length (Fig. S3B) were significantly associated with platform-level logFC, but the effect sizes were small (R2 = 0.0872 and 0.0101 respectively), indicating that neither is a primary driver of the platform difference.

Gene ontology enrichment analysis (adj. p < 0.05, goseq (Young et al., 2010)) showed that genes enriched in 10X fell into coherent, well-defined categories, whereas genes enriched in Parse 3’ mapped onto a smaller and less coherent set of terms. Because GC content contributed weakly to differential expression, we corrected for it using the Wallenius noncentral hypergeometric test. Of the terms significantly enriched in 10X, 4 were GC-driven and 78 GC-robust; of the terms enriched in Parse 3’, 23 were GC-robust and 26 were GC-driven (Fig. S3C). As many terms were redundant or related, we collapsed those with overlapping gene sets into 22 representative terms enriched in 10X and 2 in Parse 3’ (Fig. 4C).

Genes enriched in 10X were most strongly associated with the mitochondrial inner membrane (GO:0005743, adj. p ~ 10−44), reflecting the oxidative phosphorylation complexes (NDUF, COX, UQCR, ATP5/6, and SDH families) together with associated assembly factors, import machinery, and mitochondrial ribosomal proteins. This is in line with a previous finding that genes responsible for mitochondrial respiration are enriched in 10X (Sarieva et al., 2026). The next most significant representative term, Translation (GO:0006412, adj. p ~ 10−29) was driven primarily by ribosomal protein-coding genes and translation elongation factors.

Genes encoding the 26S proteasome were likewise depleted in Parse, though captured only indirectly, through extracellular exosome (GO:0070062, adj. p ~ 10−21), mitochondrial matrix (GO:0005759, adj. p ~ 10−8), cytoplasmic vesicle lumen (GO:0060205, adj. p ~ 10−6). Spliceosomal components were also captured by spliceosomal tri-snRP complex (GO:0097526, adj. p ~ 10−6).

To confirm this pattern of depletion across these abundant protein complexes, we quantified the per-cell percent-count distribution of each gene set (Fig. 5). Across all Parse datasets, the nuclear-encoded core OXPHOS genes—spanning complexes I through V (NDUF, SDH, UQCR, COX, and ATP5 families)—were depleted in Parse relative to 10X: mean OXPHOS percentage per cell ranged from 1.10% to 3.76% in 10X against 0.17% to 0.67% in Parse. The 26S proteasome genes (PSMA/B/C/D families) and the spliceosomal SNRP genes (SNRPB/D/E/F/G) followed the same trend, with a lower mean per-cell percentage in every Parse dataset than in its matching 10X dataset across all experiments.

Although 10X-enriched genes were concentrated in abundant, broadly expressed categories, this extended only weakly to constitutively transcribed housekeeping genes. Using a curated human housekeeping gene set (Hounkpe et al., 2021), 63.1% of housekeeping genes had a negative logFC (favoring 10X), against 51% of genes overall (Fig. S5A).

In contrast to 10X, Parse 3’ was enriched, generally with weaker significance, for genes encoding regulatory proteins rather than large, ubiquitous protein complexes (Fig. 4C). The GO enrichment terms clustered around three related themes: regulation of small-GTPase signaling, protein kinase activity, and chromatin and transcriptional regulation. To confirm this pattern independently of the GO annotation and across all experiments, we quantified the per-cell percent-count distribution of Rho GTPase regulator genes (prefixes DOCK, ARHGAP, and ARHGEF) in each dataset. Consistent with the differential expression result, the mean per-cell percentage of these genes was higher in every Parse dataset than in the matching 10X dataset, across all experiments.

In addition to the findings above, canonical PBMC marker genes also showed greater representation in 10X than in Parse (Fig. 4A). Most canonical markers (82%) had a negative Parse 3’/10X log-fold change, and among the subset that were highly differentially expressed (68%), all but two were enriched in 10X.

In order to confirm whether differentially expressed genes arose from differential transcript capture, as we suspect, rather than differential cell-type composition, we quantified the relative proportion of each cell type within each dataset following cell-type identification with CellTypist (Xu et al., 2023; Conde et al., 2022). Cell-type proportions were broadly similar between platforms within each comparison (Fig. S6). For Experiments 2a and 2b, proportions for 10X and Parse agreed within 3 percentage points across cell types. For Experiment 3, the difference was somewhat larger, with 10X showing evidence of megakaryocyte/platelet contamination (2.1% of cells, versus 0% in Parse); however, megakaryocytes are a small population and not the cell type associated with the markers discussed below, and T-cell proportions in this experiment differed by only 3.36% between platforms. These compositional differences, at most a few percentage points, are too small to account for log2 fold-changes of 3–6 (i.e., roughly 10- to 50-fold on a linear scale) observed between platforms for canonical immune markers in the edgePython comparison, such as the cytotoxic marker NKG7 (log2FC(Parse 3’/10X) = −5.62) or the pan-T-cell markers CD3E and CD3D (log2FC = −2.55 and −3.84, respectively).

### Differential expression analysis reveals smaller but significant differences between oligo(dT) and randO priming.

We next performed the same edgePython differential expression analysis, blocking on study of origin, comparing Parse 3’ to Parse randO reads directly, in order to isolate the effect of priming strategy independent of platform.

Unlike the 10X and Parse 3’ comparison, the Parse 3’ and randO datasets were not separated along the first dimension, accounting for 78.5% of the variance of the MDS plot (Fig. 6A), though they separated along the second dimension accounting for (18.2 %). This suggests that batch effects between experiments were larger than priming bias. Between priming strategies, 5,828 genes were significantly enriched in Parse randO and 3,984 were significantly enriched in Parse 3’ (Fig. 6B). Unlike the 10X versus Parse 3’ comparison, Parse 3’ and Parse randO did not appear to be specifically enriched for PBMC marker genes: only 54% of markers showed a positive log-fold change (randO/3’).

As with the 10X vs. Parse 3’ analysis, we performed cross-validation of differentially expressed genes between Parse 3’ and Parse randO using the mouse thymocyte datasets (Exp 4a and 4b), comparing bulk gene-level logCPM percentages (Fig. 6E and Fig. S4B respectively). This analysis revealed strong concordance with the differential expression results. Of the differentially expressed orthologs enriched in Parse 3’, 93% and 84% had a higher logCPM percentage in Parse 3’ than Parse randO in Experiments 4a and 4b, respectively. Of the differentially expressed orthologs enriched in Parse randO, 73% and 86% had a higher logCPM percentage in Parse randO than Parse 3’ in Experiments 4a and 4b, respectively.

Random hexamer primers bind along the full length of a transcript rather than only at the poly(A) tail, raising the possibility that randO priming preferentially captures longer transcripts. We found instead that the structural bias between Parse 3’ and randO reads was driven primarily by GC content rather than transcript length. In a regression of priming-strategy enrichment on these two variables, gene length explained very little variance (R2 = 0.0118) compared to GC content (R2 = 0.2997) (Fig. S7A and Fig. 6C respectively). This bias was also evident when comparing the logCPM gene percentages in the mouse thymocyte datasets (Fig. S4C and S4D).

We considered whether this GC-content bias could instead be explained by internal off-target priming of oligo(dT) primers at internal adenine-rich regions, rather than by a genuine preference of random hexamers for GC-rich sequence. Gene body coverage plots showed that Parse 3’ reads, while preferentially capturing the 3’ end of transcripts as expected, also captured internal sequence to some degree (Fig. S8). Annotating genes by the number and length of internal adenine single-nucleotide repeats (Svoboda et al., 2022) yielded a weaker R2 of 0.1889 in the same regression framework, and this association appeared to be driven primarily by the subset of genes differentially enriched in Parse 3’ (Fig. S7B).

Contrary to the expectation that random hexamer priming would be enriched for transcripts lacking a poly(A) tail, this was not consistently the case; enrichment instead tracked more directly with GC content. As an illustrative example, MALAT1 – a transcript lacking a canonical poly(A) tail – was significantly enriched in Parse 3’ rather than randO (logFC(randO/3’) = −1.24, FDR = 2.4e-5), consistent with its relatively low median transcript GC content of 38% despite the absence of a poly(A) tail. NEAT1, another non-polyadenylated transcript, was significantly enriched in randO (logFC = 0.757, FDR = 5.4e-4) and had a higher median transcript GC content of 49%, further supporting the GC-content association over presence or absence of a poly(A) tail as the driver of priming-strategy enrichment.

Enrichment analysis controlling for GC content revealed additional bias not fully explained by GC content alone. Using goseq, we found that of 82 naively significant terms enriched in Parse 3’, 54 were GC-robust, whereas of the 18 naively significant terms enriched in Parse randO, only 2 were GC-robust (Fig. S7C/D). Collapsing redundant terms left 6 representative terms enriched in Parse 3’(Fig. 6D). The three most significant Parse 3’-enriched terms—Cytoplasmic Translation (GO:0002181, adj. p ~ 10−29), Ribosome (adj. p ~ 10−9), and Mitochondrial Inner Membrane (GO:0005743, adj. p ~ 10−8)—were driven largely by ribosomal and mitochondrial ribosomal protein genes, transcriptional initiation factors, and mitochondrial respiration genes, similar to the functional gene classes enriched in 10X relative to Parse 3’ in the platform-level comparison above. The randO-enriched terms—lysosomal membrane (GO:0005765, adj. p = 0.039) and azurophil granule (GO:0042583, adj. p = 0.040) —-were only weakly significant in comparison.

As above, we performed cell-typing of the Parse 3’ and Parse randO to confirm that these shifts do not arise from difference in cell composition. Indeed, across all human PBMC experiments, cell-type percentages were consistently within one percentage point of each other across datasets. This suggests that while priming strategy does influence transcript capture, it does not result in compositional bias.

### Parse exhibits substantial markers of ambient RNA contamination, inconsistent with claims of reduced contamination relative to 10X.

Ambient RNA contamination is well characterized in droplet-based data, where several methods exist for its estimation and removal. Its extent in split-pool data is less settled, and published estimates disagree in both magnitude and mechanism (Parse Biosciences, 2026; King et al., 2026; Filippov et al., 2024). Because the available estimators have not been validated on split-pool data, we chose not to include them in this analysis. Instead, we rely on quality control metrics and ground-truth data from human-mouse mixtures.

The most direct of these is the composition of barcode space itself. Parse libraries recovered nearly all valid barcode combinations, far exceeding the number of cells loaded. Four of seven experiments recovered greater than 99.9% of possible combinations before filtering; the remaining three (Experiments 3, 4a, and 4b) recovered 97.5%, 90.8%, and 93.9% respectively. Barcode counts fell sharply after filtering, approaching the number of cells loaded, indicating that most recovered combinations correspond to low-count background rather than cells.

While barcode saturation establishes that background barcodes are abundant, it does not quantify how much background signal enters real cells. Human-mouse mixture datasets address this directly, as any cross-species counts within a barcode must originate outside the cell it labels. In an Evercode v1 mixture dataset (~7,000 cells) (Tran et al., 2022), every barcode carried cross-species counts (Fig. 7A). Restricting to barcodes with less than 10% cross-species signal, which are likely to represent singlets, median cross-species contamination was 1.2% for human barcodes (IQR 0.9–1.5%) and 2.1% for mouse barcodes (IQR 1.7–2.7%). In absolute terms, interquartile ranges were 29–57 cross-species counts for human barcodes and 38–74 for mouse barcodes. In the 90th percentile, contamination reached 80 counts for human barcodes and 102 for mouse barcodes, indicating that a subset of otherwise singlet-like barcodes carry appreciable background. An Evercode v2 mixture dataset gave comparable values (IQR 1–3%; 28–63 counts) (Fig. 7B). All of these figures are lower bounds, since intra-species contamination is undetectable by this approach and genes mapping to both genomes were excluded.

Barcodes with <10% mouse counts are labelled human (blue), those with <10% human counts are labelled mouse (red), and the remainder multiplets (grey). (B, C) As in (A), for the Parse Evercode WT v2 and 10X Genomics Chromium Single Cell 3’ human–mouse mixture datasets respectively.
